subject: venusFlytrap
pitch:
Category: Plant.
Subject: giant venus flytrap in a pot.
Style: Little Shop of Horrors.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a giant Audrey II-style Venus flytrap plant in a pot, with a basic rig including a stem chain and a jaw that can open.

I'm working out the dimensions and shapes: a terracotta pot, a thick curving green stem, and a head pod made of two fleshy lobes with spiky teeth and magenta-green coloring, hinged like jaws. I'm sketching the pot's lathe profile coordinates to get a believable rounded shape.

I'm thinking of adding a decal on the pot, maybe a playful label like "SEYMOUR'S ODD PLANTS" riffing on Little Shop of Horrors. Then I'm moving on to building the stem as a chain from a root joint at the pot, using a catmull path for the curve.

Now I'm defining an S-curve stem rising from the root joint to a head joint positioned forward and slightly tilted up, with the head sized as a large pod opening upward, and setting the stem's radius to taper from thicker at the base to thinner near the head.

For the jaw, I'm giving the head a lower lobe that stays fixed and an upper lobe hinged as a child joint, planning to build the lobes already in their open rest position in model space rather than posing them afterward.

Checking the drop clearance against the pot top confirms the lower jaw angle works fine. I'm reorienting so the head faces forward with the mouth opening toward the viewer, using symmetric jaw angles around a slight upward head tilt for a more natural pose.

For the lobes, I'm thinking through how to build a concave, bowl-like shell for each lobe—since standard materials typically only render front faces, a simple hollow sphere segment won't look right from the inside. I'm leaning toward a lathe-based bowl profile with actual wall thickness so both outer and inner surfaces render properly, then scaling that non-uniformly per part.

Defining the lathe profile points...

Actually, scaling a lathe mesh afterward is risky given uncertain orientation axes. A cleaner alternative is to use a loft instead, building the lobe as an ellipsoid-like pod by varying the cross-section width and height along the path.

For readability, each lobe becomes a flattened loft shell (the outer green bulge), plus a separate inner pink extrude of the leaf outline offset slightly inward as a pad, with a lip sweep along the rim and teeth added on top -- keeping the construction simple and blocky rather than relying on complex deformation.

Actually a loft ellipsoid won't give a clean flat inner cut, so I consider instead using a hemisphere dome for the bulbous outer shell, open at the bottom where the mouth is, then capping that opening with a flat pink disc so the inside doesn't show through to the background.

When two of these half-egg domes close together they form a full egg shape, and open they reveal flat pink inner faces with teeth along the rims, giving a clam-like look that's simple and bold. I'm scaling the hemisphere geometry non-uniformly to get the right lobe proportions, then orienting each half so its flat face points outward away from the mouth opening.

Setting up the pad...

Actually a fleshy lip rim might sell the mouth shape better -- maybe a magenta tube swept along the ellipse perimeter for a pouty edge.

For the teeth/cilia, I'm thinking spikes along the rim pointing toward the opposing lobe like Venus flytrap cilia, interlocking at the mouth opening. I'll need to pass an explicit bone reference since the spike points are generated from my own ellipse function rather than inheriting one automatically.

For the jaw structure, I'm setting up two hinge joints (upper and lower) parented to the head, each with its own aim direction, and building all mouth parts with explicit bone assignments to these joints. I also want to add interior detail like a dark throat cavity and a small pink tongue draping from the back of the lower jaw, since Audrey II's character comes mostly from the mouth rather than visible eyes.

For the trigger hairs, I'm adding three thin red-tipped spikes on each inner pad, mimicking the classic venus flytrap trigger hairs. For the base foliage, I'm planning five leaves around the pot — a mix of mini-traps on curving tendrils and broader leaf blades with petioles — and building each as a joint chain sweeping outward from the soil, using a catmull-rom curve parented to the root.

Now I'm sketching a helper for the mini traps at tendril tips, and thinking through the overall color scheme inspired by the 1986 film Audrey II — green body with purple veins and mottled blotches, thorny bumps along a thicker ribbed stem, a curling vine tendril, and big red-magenta lips.

I'm also planning details for the pot: a classic terracotta planter with a decal label, maybe referencing "Mushnik's Florist" with a small "FEED ME" tag card, plus throat colors (dark interior, pale cream teeth) and listing out the texture assets I'll need — pot label, rim stripe, and leaf vein card textures.

For the mouth interior, I'll draw a circular texture with a radial gradient from a dark throat to pink lips, adding ridge lines and spots, oriented so the hinge sits at the bottom and the tip at the top; the upper lobe gets a ridged palate look while the lower lobe reuses the texture with an added tongue shape.

Now for the dome's outer skin, I'm thinking of using UV-based noise to create radiating veins from the pole, like longitude lines mimicking a flytrap's ribs, colored dark purple against green.

1 at the equator rim, so I'll tint purple/red where v is small near the rim and use normals for warm-cool lighting variation. For the pot, I'm going terracotta with grain texture and a lighter/darker banded rim based on height, plus darker mud near the base and some whitish salt stains for realism. For soil, I'm mottling brown tones and maybe scattering a few small pebbles.

Now for the rosette leaves, I'm planning six strap-like Venus flytrap leaves swept outward from the base with Catmull-Rom curves, each arching up and out from the soil with a flattened petiole section, tipped with a small trap oriented mouth-up along the tangent direction, and each leaf getting its own joint for animation.

I'm checking that the drooping tip stays clear of the ground, then planning to alternate three open mini-traps with three broad leaf blades around the stem, orienting each leaf along its tangent direction. Now I'm defining a helper function for building these mini traps.

Setting up the stem as a curved spine with five joints running from the base through a gentle backward curve into the bulb, tapering in radius as it rises before widening into the head bulb.
